# Governance and communication {#sec-governance-communication}

## Institutional judgment and statistical optimization {#sec-governance-responsibility}

Adopting a common grade requires decisions about what the criteria represent, whose interests they serve, which errors matter and what consequences may follow. Targets, weights, withholding costs and feasible actions express some of these judgments, but minimizing the resulting loss cannot authorize their adoption. We use the preceding analysis and institutional cases to propose governance practices. These recommendations have not been tested as interventions and do not constitute a new theory of fairness.

Interpreting a grade first requires evidence about indicator validity. In the causal conception of Borsboom, Mellenbergh, and van Heerden, validity requires that the attribute exist and that variation in it cause variation in measurement outcomes; reliability or predictive adequacy does not establish either condition [@borsboom_validity_2004, pp. 1061–1063, 1067–1070]. Messick's 1994 ETS report considers the support for score meanings and their implications for use, including construct underrepresentation and irrelevant variation [@messick_validity_report_1994, pp. 1–6]. Although these conceptions differ, both require more than statistical fit to justify an interpretation.

Under either conception, the interpretation depends on the population and period represented, dimensions omitted from the reporting purpose and assumptions linking adjusted outcomes to institutional effects. Model fit alone cannot resolve these questions. Messick further distinguishes adverse consequences of valid descriptions from consequences attributable to measurement problems, so an undesirable outcome need not establish invalidity [@messick_validity_report_1994, pp. 9, 23–24]. Conversely, a precise description does not justify every action taken in response.

## Preference elicitation and decision authority {#sec-governance-preferences}

Preference elicitation requires specification of the objectives and consequences to be valued. Allocating points among criterion names gives weights no definite meaning without that specification. In the 1993 Cambridge edition, Keeney and Raiffa distinguish objectives from attributes and assess attribute sets for completeness, operational usefulness, nonredundancy and other desiderata [@keeney_raiffa_1993, pp. 31–32, 38–40, 50–52]. Their normalized additive-value examples interpret a coefficient through a specified worst-to-best improvement relative to improvements on other attributes. Calling a criterion important leaves the relevant ranges and tradeoffs unspecified [@keeney_raiffa_1993, pp. 117, 121–123].

For the reporting problem, composite coefficients $a$ combine target magnitudes, whereas directional weights $w$ value errors in criterion-specific comparisons. Interpreting either set as preference weights over intervention consequences would require a further decision model. The withholding cost separately values communicating a direction relative to leaving it unasserted. Equal numerical weights are a convention; they neither equate these meanings nor establish neutrality.

The account of each setting should identify whether it is an authorized policy judgment, an elicited preference, an analyst assumption or a sensitivity scenario. Consultation informs these choices, but adoption still requires a specified authority. In Keeney and Raiffa's interpersonal formulation, a decision maker incorporates others' evaluations and makes the final comparisons [@keeney_raiffa_1993, pp. 515–519]. Incorporating those evaluations does not transfer decision authority or establish a uniquely legitimate institutional arrangement.

The clinical illustration makes the source of the weights particularly relevant. Li and colleagues' 2019 demonstration used clinician-supplied weights for two selected patients and simulated preferences for the population display, rather than eliciting preferences from all trial participants [@li_bayesian_2019, pp. 3046–3048]. Similarly, SMAA-2 cautions that a uniform distribution over the weight simplex generally does not describe the distribution of decision makers' preferences [@lahdelma_salminen2001smaa2, p. 446]. Such analyses show which conclusions depend on contested settings. They leave disagreement about legitimate priorities unresolved and do not turn an analyst's distribution into a vote.

## Compensation across criteria {#sec-governance-compensation}

In a composite, an improvement on one dimension may offset a deterioration on another. In a weighted directional objective, the report may incur more errors on a lightly weighted criterion to reduce errors elsewhere. Each form of compensation requires institutional justification, including the circumstances in which a label may be awarded despite an adverse finding on a particular dimension.

The April 2026 CMS hospital methodology, version 5.1, combines standardized measure groups and separately restricts the highest rating through a Safety of Care condition. A hospital with at least three safety measures and a score in the specified lowest safety quartile can receive at most four stars [@CMSHospitalStars2026, pp. 17–24]. This label restriction uses its own information condition and reference population. A posterior expected-error constraint concerns a different quantity.

The criterion-specific $q$ constraints in @sec-criterion-protections bound expected wrong fractions under a declared law when disclosure is positive. These are averages over disclosed comparisons, so they impose no ceiling on every pair's error probability. Their statistical interpretation depends on the target, law and numerical feasibility certificate. They do not establish equal treatment, equitable access, absence of discrimination or acceptable consequences. Protecting a disadvantaged population may require different targets, constraints or actions; calling an error constraint a protection does not provide that policy specification.

Documentation should therefore identify substantive restrictions and error tolerances separately, together with the body adopting each. An exact grade-count requirement can make a restriction infeasible. Resolving that incompatibility requires an explicit reconsideration of the requirements, since an undocumented relaxation would conceal a policy change. Extensive withholding can alternatively satisfy an error constraint at the expense of usefulness. Even where the mathematical consequences are known, choosing this tradeoff remains an institutional responsibility.

## Precision, need and intervention benefit {#sec-governance-precision-need}

Precision concerns how well the evidence resolves a target; need concerns the target or policy problem; benefit concerns the consequences of an action. An association among them does not make them interchangeable. A small institution may have less informative data without having less need, and the institution with the greatest estimated need may not benefit most from the available intervention. Thus selecting by expected need differs from selecting by expected treatment benefit, just as reliable comparative reporting differs from filling a fixed budget (@sec-selection-benchmarks).

England's IMD25 treats precision and normative weights separately at the measurement stage. The 2025 technical report describes empirical Bayesian shrinkage for many unstable component indicators, while retaining substantive domain weights and transformations [@mclennan2025imdtechnical, §§3.4, 3.6–3.7, appendix C]. Greater measurement precision does not itself determine a domain's normative weight. The report's downstream use also matters: the March 2026 Pride in Place expansion methodology combines deprivation with community need and applies geographic eligibility and distribution constraints. Its selection rule documents an announced allocation, not realized programme effects [@mhclg2026prideexpansion, methodological principles and steps 1–5].

Precision information may enter both the likelihood and the target distribution, especially when it is associated with substantive characteristics [@gu2023invidious, §5, pp. 19–21]. The model specification should describe this choice. Strong shrinkage and narrow intervals are properties of the analysis and do not measure deservingness. Nor does uncertainty require identical grades: the chosen report depends jointly on targets, pairwise relations, preferences and feasible actions, rather than on a unit's standard error alone.

The Head Start regulatory snapshot, current through 22 October 2026, separates eligibility, locally established selection criteria and enrollment; it prescribes no national posterior grade [@hhsHeadStartEligibilitySelection2026, §§1302.12–1302.15]. A report of uncertain need would leave those requirements in force and would not establish expected developmental gains for a child. Likewise, the audit-population contact gap in @sec-employer-reporting supports a descriptive employer comparison, without by itself constituting a legal finding or estimating the effect of publication.

## Interpretation of withheld comparisons {#sec-governance-withholding}

A shared grade withholds an internal direction. It establishes neither equality nor equivalence, negligible differences or absence of need. The reason for withholding may be uncertainty, criterion conflict, error costs or structural restrictions on a coherent common report. Interpretation therefore requires the reporting rule; the units cannot generally be described as indistinguishable. Similarly, an earlier grade does not assert superiority on every criterion.

The institutional rule must also specify the response to a withheld comparison, such as retaining the current action, seeking more information, reviewing the case or applying a separate allocation procedure. The statistical model alone cannot justify that choice. Inaction may have consequences when services or investigations are time-sensitive, while additional evidence can be costly and may leave substantive criterion conflict unresolved. Valuing these consequences requires a decision model beyond the reporting loss.

Under the equality-neutral extension, a guard can require the same grade for units whose entire active target profiles are justifiably equal. The published grade cannot establish that equality. Sharing one contextual value is insufficient when another positively weighted criterion differs, and units outside a common equality class may still receive the same grade. Reports should therefore state the loss convention, active criteria and evidence for any structural equality restriction. The preservation result in @prp-tie-aware-guard establishes a reporting optimum under its stated conditions, without establishing equal treatment, causal benefit or an invariant funding schedule.

Selecting a fixed number of units requires a further rule, whether a boundary lottery, an additional priority criterion or a constrained selection procedure. Each defines a new action and needs its own justification. The exact-budget results in @sec-selection-benchmarks show why an optimal report need not yield an optimal allocation. Randomized mixtures used to compare frontiers at matched expected disclosure likewise serve an analytical purpose; they are not recommendations to alternate published grades.

A withheld comparison must also be distinguished from missing or ineligible data. Placing an excluded unit in the lowest grade asserts adverse comparisons against it. Suppression should instead use an explicit status outside the grade scale, so that an unfavorable assessed position is distinguishable from an inability or lack of authorization to assess the unit.

## Documentation and correction {#sec-governance-transparency-appeal}

A readable explanation should identify the target, population, period and meaning of the grades. A technical supplement can record data versions, transformations, producer assumptions, origins of weights, action restrictions, numerical certificates and error denominators. Together these accounts allow readers to understand an earlier grade and examine how it was constructed. Providing them need not disclose protected individual information.

An appeal may concern an incorrect input, a measurement interpretation, a computational error or an authorized priority. These require different responses. Correcting an enrollment count may warrant reproducible recalculation, whereas changing a criterion's weight requires a decision by the body responsible for the policy. Because grades are selected jointly, correcting one institution's input may alter other institutions' grades. A revision should therefore retain the cohort and model version and explain those wider consequences.

The process should identify who receives challenges, which evidence is admissible, who decides each type of challenge and how corrections and unresolved disagreements are recorded. Correcting an existing release also differs from adopting a policy for future releases. We recommend these arrangements for traceability and accountability without claiming that the cited statistical methods implement appeals or that a particular process improves outcomes.

Sensitivity analysis can assist review by identifying conclusions that depend on disputed assumptions. Keeney and Raiffa discuss concentrating assessment on difficult tradeoffs [@keeney_raiffa_1993, pp. 123–125]. Preference-learning methods also depend on assumptions: in Ru and colleagues' sorting formulation, incompatibility between supposedly certain examples and the model calls for reconsideration [@ru2023sorting, §4.4, pp. 604–605]. Treating the disputed preference as noise may otherwise conceal disagreement about the model or the authority adopting it.

## Illustrative report explanation and uncertainty statement {#sec-model-report-explanation}

For illustration, consider the following explanation of criterion-weighted grades in a hypothetical service-need report. It represents neither a fitted application nor a new numerical example. An institutional release would replace the unspecified criteria, population, period, settings and review arrangements with its own.

“We compare service units on the stated dimensions of unmet need. An earlier grade reports higher priority under the adopted criterion-weighted reporting rule. We use the published weights to value comparison errors on each dimension and balance those errors against withholding comparisons. An earlier grade does not mean greater need on every dimension. For units in the same grade, we leave the direction of comparison unspecified; we do not conclude that the units are equal. The criterion profiles remain available to show where the dimensions agree or conflict.

“These grades inform review and planning. They do not determine eligibility, funding, or a legal conclusion. Any allocation follows the separately published selection rule, including its budget and eligibility conditions. A unit without sufficient or eligible reporting information receives an explanatory status, not the lowest need grade. Questions about recorded data can be submitted through the stated correction process; questions about criterion definitions or priorities go to the body that adopted them.”

An accompanying statement can explain the uncertainty:

“We calculate the expected error summaries under the stated statistical model using the information available for this release. They summarize possible errors in the comparisons that this report actually discloses. They are not observed counts of mistakes, a promise that each comparison meets the average error level, or a probability that every published comparison is correct. When no comparisons are disclosed, the disclosed-error fraction is undefined; silence is not reported as perfect accuracy.

“The results may change with corrected data, another defensible model, or different authorized priorities. The technical account separates uncertainty represented by the model, sensitivity to preferences, and numerical approximation. A certificate that the calculation meets its stated optimization tolerance does not establish that the model or the criteria are substantively correct. The report does not estimate the benefit of an intervention unless a separate, explicitly justified analysis supplies that target.”

An illustrative communication design for a hypothetical service-need report. The schematic grade pattern explains what an earlier grade and a shared grade communicate; it is not calculated from data. A separate unassessed status avoids turning missing or ineligible information into an adverse grade. The public explanation is linked to a versioned technical record and an uncertainty statement. Proposed challenge routes distinguish correcting inputs or computations from reconsidering criterion meanings or authorized priorities. Eligibility, allocation and intervention benefit require separate decisions. No actual provider, institutional procedure, funding outcome or tested policy benefit is represented.
:::

This explanation identifies the report's claim and the assumptions that readers may challenge. The adopting body must still choose whether to publish the grade, seek more evidence or pursue a different objective. These decisions return to @sec-public-decisions: the interpretation of what is communicated and withheld precedes institutional action. In @sec-synthesis-agenda we bring together the results and questions for further research.
